questions.q: Given `var incident = { number: "INC001", priority: 1 };`, what does `incident.priority` return?
options: An error, because incident has no numeric index
questions.explain: Dot notation reads the value stored at the named property - priority holds the value 1.

options: Bracket notation is required for every object, always
Dot notation only works on arrays, not objects
Bracket notation lets the property name be decided at runtime, from whatever the variable fieldName holds - incident.fieldName would not work
There is no difference; both are purely stylistic
questions.explain: incident.fieldName would look for a literal property called "fieldName", which doesn't exist. incident[fieldName] evaluates the variable first, looking up "priority".
Chaining dot notation first retrieves the assignedTo object, then reads its name property, returning "Jordan Lee".

questions.q: What is the difference between how an array and an object are typically accessed?
options: Arrays and objects are accessed identically, by numeric index only
An array is accessed by numeric index (position); an object is accessed by named property
Objects are accessed by numeric index; arrays are accessed by name
Neither can be accessed after creation
questions.explain: Arrays use ordered numeric positions starting at 0. Objects use named keys (properties), not positions.

questions.q: Why does object shape matter for the ServiceNow work ahead in this course, per this lesson?
options: ServiceNow doesn't use objects or JSON at all
GlideRecord fields and REST API JSON responses are both shaped like nested objects, so comfort with plain object properties now makes that later material click
Objects will be replaced entirely by a ServiceNow-specific syntax
Object notation is only used for styling, not data
questions.explain: Chapter 2 onward works heavily with GlideRecord and JSON, both of which are structured as nested objects - exactly what this lesson builds fluency in first.
